title: “WE WALK BY FAITH, NOT BY SIGHT” — THE VERSE YOU'VE BEEN TAUGHT TO USE FOR YOUR DREAMS WAS ACTUALLY WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING FAR MORE SERIOUS
paragraphs: “WE WALK BY FAITH, NOT BY SIGHT” — THE VERSE YOU'VE BEEN TAUGHT TO USE FOR YOUR DREAMS WAS ACTUALLY WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING FAR MORE SERIOUS

What if the words you've been repeating to encourage yourself were never primarily about achieving the impossible, becoming successful, or getting everything you've prayed for? What if Paul was talking about something that could completely change the way you face suffering, disappointment, unanswered prayers, and even death?
There is a kind of faith that can shout when the doors are opening.
But what happens when every door stays closed?
What happens when the medical report doesn't change?
When the person you prayed would stay walks away?
When the business you believed God would bless collapses?
When you've been faithful, you've been praying, you've been giving, you've been waiting... and the miracle you expected still hasn't arrived?
Can you still say you trust God?
Not because you're certain tomorrow will bring the breakthrough.
Not because you've received a supernatural confirmation that everything will work out exactly as you imagined.
But because Jesus Christ is still Lord, even when your circumstances seem to tell a different story.
That is where one of the most frequently quoted verses in Christianity becomes far more uncomfortable, far more beautiful, and far more powerful than many of us have realized.
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.” — 2 Corinthians 5:7 (KJV)
You've probably seen those words printed on shirts, framed on bedroom walls, written in social media biographies, and attached to inspirational messages about chasing enormous dreams.
Someone wants to become a millionaire.
“Walk by faith, not by sight.”
Someone wants to launch a business without sufficient resources.
“Walk by faith, not by sight.”
Someone believes a relationship is destined to happen despite every warning sign.
“Walk by faith, not by sight.”
And sometimes the message underneath it all becomes something like this:
If you believe strongly enough, the impossible thing you're imagining will eventually become your reality.
But there is a serious problem.
That is not what the apostle Paul was primarily teaching.

And when we finally read his words in their original context, we discover something that may confront our ambitions, expose our fears, and restore a kind of faith that doesn't collapse when life refuses to follow our plans.
Because Paul wasn't writing a motivational speech about achieving personal greatness.
He was writing about mortality.
Suffering.
The resurrection.
The temporary nature of this earthly life.
And the staggering reality that a believer can face death with confidence because Jesus Christ has already conquered the grave.
Read that again.
The verse we've sometimes turned into a slogan for earthly success was written in a passage about our eternal home.
And that changes everything.
Imagine a woman sitting alone in a hospital corridor at two in the morning.
Her hands are trembling.
Her Bible is open.
Her husband is inside a room surrounded by machines, and the doctors have already explained that the situation is serious.
She has prayed.
Her church has prayed.
Her family has prayed.
She believes God is powerful enough to heal him.
But she doesn't know what will happen next.
Then she looks down and reads:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
What does that verse mean to her?
Does it mean she must declare with absolute certainty that her husband will recover?
Does it mean that acknowledging the possibility of death would somehow betray her faith?
Does it mean that if the healing doesn't come, she didn't believe strongly enough?
No.
And anyone who has ever stood beside a hospital bed, buried someone they loved, or watched a prayer remain unanswered needs to understand why.
Biblical faith is not the power to force God to fulfill our preferred outcome. It is confidence in the God who remains faithful regardless of the outcome.
That distinction is not small.
It can mean the difference between a faith rooted in Jesus Christ and a faith quietly built around our own expectations.
Now listen carefully to Paul's actual words.
In the original Greek, 2 Corinthians 5:7 reads:
διὰ πίστεως γὰρ περιπατοῦμεν, οὐ διὰ εἴδους
Transliterated:
dia pisteōs gar peripatoumen, ou dia eidous.
A close translation is:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
The Greek word πίστεως (pisteōs) comes from πίστις (pistis), meaning faith, trust, or confidence.
The verb περιπατοῦμεν (peripatoumen) literally refers to walking, but it can also describe the way someone lives or conducts their life.
And εἴδους (eidous) refers to visible appearance or what is seen.
Paul is describing the present condition of believers who trust God's promises while they have not yet entered the fullness of what those promises anticipate.
He is not teaching that observable facts are meaningless.
He is not commanding Christians to ignore wisdom, evidence, medical advice, or practical responsibility.
He is not saying that every strong desire in your heart is a divine promise waiting to manifest.
He is explaining that Christians presently live by trusting the Lord whom they do not yet see face to face.
And the verses surrounding this statement make that meaning unmistakable.
In 2 Corinthians 5:1, Paul writes:
Our earthly house.
Our temporary dwelling.
Our mortal existence.
Paul is talking about the frailty of our present bodies and the hope God has given us beyond death.
And in the preceding chapter, he writes:
There it is.
The contrast.
The visible and the eternal.
The present and the promised.
The suffering we experience now and the glory God has prepared for those who belong to Christ.
Paul was not saying, “Believe hard enough and your dream house will become yours.”
He was saying, in effect, “Even when this earthly life is wasting away, our hope remains secure in the eternal promises of God.”
And consider who was writing those words.
This was not a man sitting comfortably in a palace, enjoying uninterrupted prosperity while explaining how to become successful.
This was Paul.
A servant of Jesus Christ who knew imprisonment, beatings, rejection, danger, hunger, exhaustion, and suffering.
In 2 Corinthians 4:8–9, he describes believers as troubled, perplexed, persecuted, and cast down—yet not destroyed.
His faith had been tested in places where shallow optimism could never have survived.
And still he wrote:
“We walk by faith, not by sight.”
Why?
Because the resurrection of Jesus Christ had changed what suffering and death ultimately meant.
Paul knew that the worst thing this fallen world could do to his body could not overturn the promises of the risen Savior.
He knew that what he could see was not the whole story.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
Because somewhere along the way, you may have begun measuring God's faithfulness by how many of your expectations He fulfills.
When the money comes, God is good.
When the diagnosis improves, God is good.
When the relationship works, God is good.
When the opportunity opens, God is good.
But what happens when the answer is no?
What happens when you obey God and still lose something precious?
What happens when the righteous suffer and the wicked appear to prosper?
What happens when you have done everything you know to do, and heaven seems silent?
Is Jesus still worthy of your trust?
That question reaches deeper than any motivational quote ever could.
Because the Christian life is not built on a promise that you will escape every disappointment.
It is built on the crucified and risen Son of God.
And the cross itself confronts our obsession with visible success.
Think about Calvary.
If you had stood there on that Friday, watching Jesus mocked, beaten, and crucified, what would your eyes have told you?
Defeat.
Humiliation.
Failure.
The Messiah hanging between criminals.
His followers scattered.
His enemies celebrating.
His body wounded.
His blood poured out.
From the perspective of ordinary human sight, it looked as though darkness had won.
But what looked like defeat was the place where the sinless Savior was giving His life for sinners.
What looked like humiliation was part of God's saving purpose.
What looked like the end was followed by an empty tomb.
The cross teaches us that appearances cannot always tell us what God is accomplishing.
But we must be careful here.
That does not mean every disappointment is secretly a guarantee that God will give us something bigger on earth.
It does not mean every closed door will eventually reopen.
It does not mean every financial loss will be repaid with wealth.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored in the way we desire.
The resurrection of Jesus guarantees something far greater than the fulfillment of every personal ambition.
It establishes our hope that sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
And that hope is not wishful thinking.
It is rooted in the historical proclamation at the center of the Christian faith: Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Now consider something else.
Even Jesus, in the garden of Gethsemane, prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39 (KJV)
Do you see the surrender?
Jesus did not teach us to treat prayer as a way of commanding the Father to fulfill our preferences.
He showed perfect obedience to the Father's will.
His prayer was not a failure of faith.
It was the expression of holy submission.
And if the sinless Son of God prayed in surrender to the Father, why have we sometimes been taught that surrendering our preferred outcome means we lack faith?
Why have we made certainty about an earthly result the measure of spiritual maturity?
Why do we sometimes tell grieving people that they simply need to believe harder?
There is a kind of religious language that sounds powerful until it meets a funeral.
A kind of preaching that sounds victorious until the treatment fails.
A kind of theology that promises everything except the strength to remain faithful when suffering comes.
But the Gospel is not that fragile.
Jesus never promised His disciples a life without tribulation.
He said:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33 (KJV)
Notice what He did not say.
He did not say you would never experience pain.
He did not say every prayer would receive the answer you wanted.
He did not say following Him would make you wealthy, admired, comfortable, or immune to tragedy.
He said that in this world, trouble would come.
And then He gave His followers a reason to have courage.
Not because the world would always become easier.
But because He had overcome it.
That is the difference between faith centered on Christ and faith centered on outcomes.
One says, “I trust God because I know He will give me what I want.”
The other says, “I trust God because Jesus Christ has proven Himself worthy, even when I cannot understand what He allows.”
One collapses when expectations fail.
The other grieves, wrestles, cries, asks questions, and sometimes trembles—but keeps returning to the Savior.
And please understand this.
Walking by faith does not mean you never cry.
It does not mean you never feel afraid.
It does not mean you never struggle with questions.
It does not mean you have to pretend that losing someone you love doesn't hurt.
The Bible gives us psalms of lament.
It shows us prophets overwhelmed by sorrow.
It shows us Job sitting in ashes.
It shows us David asking God how long his suffering will continue.
And it shows us Jesus weeping at the tomb of Lazarus.
Tears are not automatic evidence of unbelief.
Sometimes faith looks like worship.
Sometimes faith looks like obedience.
And sometimes faith looks like a brokenhearted person whispering, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief,” echoing Mark 9:24.
Perhaps you've been there.
Perhaps you're there right now.
You still believe Jesus is Lord.
You still believe Scripture is true.
But you're tired.
You're carrying questions you don't know how to ask in church.
You're watching other people celebrate answers to prayer while you are still waiting.
And privately, you're wondering whether something is wrong with your faith.
You hear testimonies about promotions, weddings, healings, and financial breakthroughs.
You celebrate with others because you genuinely love them.
But then you go home.
You close the door.
And you ask God why your story seems so different.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Your suffering does not automatically mean God has abandoned you.
Paul's own life makes that clear.
In 2 Corinthians 12, he describes a painful affliction that he pleaded with the Lord to remove.
Three times he prayed.
But the Lord did not grant the removal he requested.
Instead, Paul received this answer:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
Imagine that.
An apostle.
A man who had witnessed extraordinary works of God.
A man who preached Christ with remarkable courage.
And still, he had to live with an affliction he had asked God to take away.
Was Paul's faith defective?
No.
The passage teaches us something profound about grace.
Sometimes God displays His sustaining power not by removing every weakness, but by enabling His people to endure through dependence on Christ.
This is not a command to stop praying for healing.
Pray.
Ask.
Seek medical care when needed.
Receive wise counsel.
Work diligently.
Pursue opportunities.
Trust that God is able to do extraordinary things.
But never confuse God's ability to do something with His promise that He will do it in exactly the way you desire.
Faith is not permission to invent promises God never made.
And faithfulness is not measured by the size of the dream you pursue.
You can have enormous ambitions and still be spiritually lost.
You can accomplish everything you once imagined and still be empty before God.
Jesus asked:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36 (KJV)
That question should interrupt us.
Because what if you achieve the dream...
Build the house...
Grow the company...
Earn the applause...
Gain the followers...
And still never truly surrender your life to Jesus Christ?
What if the greatest tragedy is not that you failed to become who you wanted to be?
What if it is that you succeeded in becoming everything you wanted while neglecting the One who gave His life to save you?
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to positive thinking with Bible verses attached.
The Gospel begins with a truth our pride does not naturally want to hear.
We are sinners in need of reconciliation with a holy God.
We cannot purchase forgiveness through religious performance.
We cannot earn salvation through charitable giving.
We cannot become righteous before God by building a successful life.
We need a Savior.
And God, in His mercy, has provided one.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
Grace.
Not achievement.
Not personal greatness.
Not financial success.
Not the number of dreams you managed to accomplish.
Grace.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) carries the meaning of grace or favor, and in this passage Paul emphasizes that salvation is God's gift, not something we can claim as our own accomplishment.
That is why the message of Jesus Christ is so different from the world's endless demand to prove your worth.
The world tells you to build a life impressive enough to be admired.
The Gospel tells you that you cannot save yourself, but Christ came to save sinners.
The world tells you to chase a version of yourself that never fails.
The Gospel calls you to repent, believe, and follow the Savior who died and rose again.
The world tells you that your greatest problem is that you have not yet achieved your potential.
Scripture tells us our deepest problem is sin—and our greatest need is reconciliation with God.
And Jesus Christ is the answer.
Not because He promises to turn every earthly desire into reality.
But because He came to redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Consider Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His miracles.
He had boldly declared that he would remain loyal.
And then, when the pressure came, he denied knowing his Lord.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering your own voice saying you did not know the One you had promised never to abandon.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine meeting Jesus' eyes, as Luke 22 records, and going outside to weep bitterly.
Peter's failure was not imaginary.
His denial was real.
His sin mattered.
But that was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Grace met a fallen disciple and called him back to faithful service.
That is the beauty of redemption.
Jesus does not need to rewrite history by pretending our sins were harmless.
He redeems sinners through His mercy, forgiveness, and transforming power.
And perhaps that is the part of this message that touches the place you've been hiding.
Because maybe your greatest struggle isn't a dream that hasn't come true.
Maybe it's a past you wish you could erase.
A decision that damaged your family.
A season of compromise.
A secret sin.
A betrayal.
An addiction.
A bitterness you've allowed to grow.
A spiritual life that looks convincing in public but feels empty when nobody is watching.
Maybe you know all the right Christian phrases.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
You know how to encourage others.
But deep inside, you know there are places in your heart you've resisted surrendering to Jesus.
And perhaps you've been using faith language to avoid repentance.
Believing for a bigger future while refusing to confront the sin destroying your present.
Asking God to open doors while ignoring the commands He has already given.
Declaring victory while quietly making peace with the very things Christ calls you to leave behind.
Friend, there is no freedom in pretending.
And there is no need to keep running from the Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
You do not need a more impressive religious image.
You need Jesus.
You need His forgiveness.
You need His truth.
You need the transforming work of His grace.
And the same Christ who restored Peter still calls sinners to turn from sin and follow Him.
Not because sin is unimportant.
But because His mercy is real.
Not because repentance earns His love.
But because genuine faith does not want to keep making a home in the darkness.
And this is why walking by faith is so much more demanding than simply believing something extraordinary will happen.
It means trusting Jesus enough to obey Him when obedience costs you something.
It means telling the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
It means refusing dishonest gain even when money is desperately needed.
It means forgiving someone who hurt you, while still maintaining wise and necessary boundaries.
It means turning away from sin even when nobody else knows about it.
It means choosing integrity when compromise would make life easier.
It means loving your enemies, caring for the vulnerable, and refusing to exchange biblical truth for public approval.
It means holding your possessions with open hands because this world is not your permanent home.
It means remembering that your identity is not ultimately determined by your bank account, your relationship status, your career, your health, or your popularity.
It is found in your relationship to Jesus Christ.
And if you belong to Him, your future rests in a promise far greater than earthly success.
Listen to Paul's words just a few verses after our original passage:
“We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.” — 2 Corinthians 5:8 (KJV)
There is the destination of Paul's argument.
Being with the Lord.
Not possessing everything this world can offer.
Not living a life without suffering.
Not accomplishing every ambition.
Being with Christ.
And the Christian hope does not end with a disembodied existence.
Paul's wider teaching, especially in 1 Corinthians 15, looks toward the resurrection of the dead through the victory of Jesus Christ.
God's ultimate purpose for His redeemed people is not merely to make this present life more comfortable.
It is to bring them into the fullness of life with Him.
Now read 2 Corinthians 5:7 again.
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
Doesn't it sound different now?
It is not smaller than you thought.
It is infinitely bigger.
Because earthly dreams, even good ones, can be lost.
Businesses can fail.
Bodies can weaken.
Money can disappear.
Relationships can break.
Reputations can crumble.
And eventually, every earthly life comes to an end.
But Jesus Christ has conquered death.
And the believer's ultimate hope rests in Him.
This is not an invitation to abandon your responsibilities or stop pursuing worthwhile goals.
Scripture commends diligence, wise planning, honest work, generosity, and stewardship.
You may pursue an education.
Build a business.
Create something beautiful.
Provide for your family.
Serve your community.
Pray boldly for healing.
Work toward a dream that honors God.
But those pursuits must never become the foundation of your faith.
Christ must remain the foundation.
And when your plans conflict with His Word, His Word must have the final authority.
When your desires become idols, repentance is necessary.
When success tempts you toward pride, remember grace.
When suffering tempts you toward despair, remember the resurrection.
When the future looks uncertain, remember who holds your eternal hope.
Because walking by faith is not walking without truth.
It is walking in the truth God has revealed, trusting Him for what you cannot yet see.
And perhaps tonight you need to release a burden you were never meant to carry.
The burden of believing that if you pray perfectly enough, every tragedy can be prevented.
The burden of thinking that if you never doubt, nothing painful will happen.
The burden of imagining that God's love must be proven through your prosperity.
The burden of pretending you are always spiritually strong.
You can lay those burdens down.
You can pray with tears.
You can ask questions.
You can seek help.
You can grieve honestly.
You can confess sin.
You can repent.
You can begin again in obedience to Christ.
And you can trust that the God who raised Jesus from the dead has not made His eternal promises dependent on your ability to control tomorrow.
Maybe the breakthrough you most desperately need is not another opportunity.
Maybe it is repentance.
Maybe it is the courage to surrender an idol.
Maybe it is freedom from a false picture of God.
Maybe it is discovering that Jesus is enough even when the answer to your prayer is not what you hoped.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop asking only, “Lord, will You give me what I want?”
And begin asking:
“Lord Jesus, teach me to want what honors You.”
“Teach me to trust Your Word.”
“Teach me to obey when obedience is difficult.”
“Teach me to remember eternity when this world overwhelms me.”
“Forgive me for treating You as a means to an earthly dream rather than worshiping You as my Lord and Savior.”
That prayer may not make you famous.
It may not make you wealthy.
It may not impress the people around you.
But a heart surrendered to Jesus Christ is not a wasted life.
And there is something deeply beautiful about a believer who can say, through tears:

“Lord, I do not understand everything that has happened. I do not know what tomorrow holds. I cannot promise that I will never feel afraid. But I know that Jesus died for my sins and rose again. I know Your Word is true. And by Your grace, I will keep following You.”
That is not weak faith.
That is faith being exercised in the very circumstances where sight offers little comfort.
And perhaps someone you know desperately needs this truth.
The friend who has begun to believe that God rejected them because their prayers weren't answered.
The mother quietly grieving.
The father exhausted from providing for his family.
The young believer confused by promises of effortless prosperity.
The Christian who feels ashamed because their life doesn't resemble the success stories they see online.
The person who stopped attending church because they thought suffering meant they had failed God.
Not because sharing a post earns God's approval, but because biblical truth deserves to reach people who may have been carrying unnecessary spiritual burdens for years.
And if these words have confronted something personal, don't rush past that conviction.
You do not have to reveal private details.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Return to it when disappointment tempts you to question God's goodness.
Return to 2 Corinthians 4 and 5.
Read the chapters for yourself.
Let Scripture, not a motivational slogan, shape what you believe.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who is struggling, the person who has drifted from church, and even the skeptic who may be willing to consider what the Gospel actually teaches.
Because our purpose is not simply to collect inspirational sayings.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ.
And that mission needs more than an occasional moment of inspiration.
It needs ongoing discipleship.
It needs Scripture carefully taught.
It needs believers who are willing to encourage one another, pray for one another, and support the faithful communication of the Gospel.
That is why Gospel Warrior is continuing to build resources for people who want to grow deeper in Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Christian faith, and develop a more consistent life of discipleship.
And if Gospel Warrior has been part of your spiritual growth, there is a meaningful way you can help this ministry continue reaching others.
Not because a payment can purchase spiritual favor.
The Gospel of Jesus Christ is not for sale.
But Scripture does teach the value of generous, willing support for the work of the Gospel.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
A cheerful giver.
Christian generosity is meant to flow from gratitude and love, not pressure, guilt, or fear.
Your local church and its spiritual care cannot be replaced by a Facebook page.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus Christ is.
The greater purpose is to continue making Scripture-centered resources available and encouraging people toward deeper faith, genuine repentance, and a life of obedience to Christ.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Use the free resources.
Encourage another believer.
And above all, keep your eyes on Jesus Christ.
Because the goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Christ known.
One life confronted by Scripture.
One sinner called to repentance.
One exhausted believer reminded of God's promises.
One wounded heart directed toward the Savior.
One family opening the Bible again.
One person discovering that the Gospel is not a promise of earthly perfection, but the good news of redemption through Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, I want you to think about one final thing.
One day, the earthly dreams you are so worried about today will no longer be the center of your attention.
The possessions you fought to acquire will remain behind.
The applause you worked so hard to receive will grow silent.
The titles you earned will no longer define you.
The approval of strangers will no longer matter.
And the question that will matter infinitely more than whether you achieved everything you wanted will be whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Not whether your life looked successful.
Not whether every prayer was answered the way you expected.
Not whether you managed to impress the world.
But whether you have repented and placed your trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
Because when Paul said we walk by faith and not by sight, he was pointing toward a hope that even death cannot destroy.
And that is the faith worth living for.
The faith worth suffering for.
The faith worth passing on to your children.
The faith worth holding onto when your hands are trembling and your eyes are filled with tears.
So dream, if your dreams honor God.
Work diligently.
Pray boldly.
Love generously.
Serve faithfully.
But never make the fulfillment of your dreams the condition of your trust in Jesus.
And never mistake a comfortable life for the ultimate reward of following Him.
The greatest gift of the Gospel is not that Jesus helps you obtain everything you want.
The greatest gift is that through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and given eternal life.
And if you've been building your faith around the things you hope God will give you, perhaps today is the day to return to the One who gave Himself for you.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become successful.
Not after you finally get your life together.
Today.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Bring Him your sin.
Bring Him your pride.
Bring Him your disappointments.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him the broken pieces of the life you thought you would have.
And follow Him.
Because the Gospel was never about turning Jesus into the servant of our dreams.
It is about sinners being rescued by grace and learning to live for the glory of their Savior.
You may never see every dream come true in this life—but through Jesus Christ, you can possess a hope that will still be standing when everything you can see has passed away.
